title: Where to and where from: -ga and -dan
goal: Show direction and origin with two endings, name your means of transport with *bilan*, and ask the way without getting lost.
bekal: attach *-ga* for destinations and *-dan* for origins
recognize how *-ga* hardens to *-ka* and *-qa* after k, q, and gʻ
say "by bus" as *avtobus bilan* — literally "with the bus"

dialogs.title: Dialog — Aeroportga qanday boraman?
dialogs.intro: Budi has to pick up a friend at the airport. He asks the receptionist at the dormitory.

lines.id: Excuse me, how do I get to the airport?

lines.speaker: Xodim:
lines.text: Metro bilan boring. Bu yerdan oʻn besh daqiqa.

notes: **-ga covers three meanings at once: to, toward, and for.** *Aeroportga* (to the airport), *haydovchiga* (to the driver), *menga* (for me). English uses different words; Uzbek uses one ending.
**Taksiga oʻtirmoq literally means "to sit into a taxi".** Uzbek uses *-ga* for getting into a vehicle, and *-dan* for getting out of one: *avtobusdan tushmoq* (to get off the bus).
**Bilan means "with" and "by".** *Doʻstim bilan* (with my friend), *metro bilan* (by metro), *qalam bilan* (with a pen). It stands **after** the noun, like almost every Uzbek function word.

**Xavotir olmang = "don't worry"**, literally "don't take worry". Uzbek often builds verbs from a noun + *olmoq/qilmoq/bermoq*: *dam olmoq* (to rest), *ish qilmoq* (to work), *yordam bermoq* (to help) — like English "take a rest", "do work", "give help".

grammars.title: -ga: destination, recipient, and deadline
body: The second of six endings. Its basic form is *-ga*, but it hardens when the word before it ends in a throat sound.
after: The hardening rule is short: **after -q and -gʻ, the ending becomes -qa; after -k, it becomes -ka.** Notice too that the last letter of the base word blends in: *togʻ* → *to**qqa***, *tok* → *to**kka***.
*-ga* also marks a **time limit**: *soat uchga* (by three o'clock), *dushanbaga* (for Monday). And it's used for prices per unit: *bir kiloga yigirma ming* (twenty thousand per kilo).
⚠️ Pronouns change slightly: *men* → *men**ga***, *sen* → *sen**ga***, *u* → *un**ga***, *biz* → *biz**ga***, *siz* → *siz**ga***, *ular* → *ular**ga***. Only *u* isn't what you'd expect.

grammars.title: -dan: from, since, through, and than
body: The third ending. Its form never changes — always *-dan*, with no exceptions.

after: The question words are *qayerdan* (from where), *kimdan* (from whom), *nimadan* (from what), *qachondan* (since when).
Pronouns follow the same pattern as with *-ga*: *mendan, sendan, undan, bizdan, sizdan, ulardan*.
Now you have three place endings at once. Practice all three as one package with every new noun: *uy — uyda — uyga — uydan*. Ten seconds, and "in", "to", and "from" are all covered.

blocks.text: The Tashkent Metro opened in 1977, the first in Central Asia, and its stations are decorated like palaces — mosaics, chandeliers, marble. Taking photos was banned until 2018; now the metro is a tourist attraction in its own right.

⚠️ *Manzil* means **address** or **destination** — from the Arabic *manzil* (stopping place, lodging) — and *safar* is the Arabic *safar* (journey), the root of English *safari*. Two words with a long history along the Silk Road.
Eight phrases that cover almost every lost-in-town situation.

Learn the direction words separately, since they often appear alone: *oʻng* (right), *chap* (left), *toʻgʻri* (straight, correct). Note that *toʻgʻri* also means "right, correct" — *Toʻgʻri!* is the most common way to agree with something.
